cues.text: You press 7, +, 5 and =. The keyboard sends the key presses to the CPU. That is input.
The CPU stores 7 and 5 in memory, two cells on the counter. That is storage.
The CPU reads 7 and 5 back from memory and adds them. That is processing.
The CPU sends 12 to the screen. The screen draws the number. That is output.
You close the app. The memory cells clear. Nothing was written to the disk, so nothing is kept.
Ada double-clicks notes.txt. The text editor asks the operating system to open the file by its path.
The operating system starts at the root, the single slash at the top of the tree.
It follows the path one folder at a time: Users, then ada, then Documents.
In Documents it finds the file. The path led to exactly one file: notes.txt.
The contents live on the disk. The operating system asks the disk driver to read the file.
The disk copies the 40 bytes of notes.txt into memory, where the CPU can reach them fast.
The editor reads the text from memory and draws it on the screen. Ada can now edit it.
You type www.wikipedia.org and press Enter. The browser needs the IP address of that name.
The browser asks DNS, the directory of the internet. DNS answers with the number 208.80.154.224.
The browser sends the request GET / to that address, through the home router and across the internet.
The server reads the request, finds the page in its files, and builds the response.
The response travels back the same way. It starts with the status code 200, which means OK.
The browser reads the text and draws the page. The clock stops at 200 milliseconds.
A program is a list of instructions. The computer reads them in order, one line at a time.
Line 1 runs: set largest to the first number, 4.
Line 2 starts the loop. n is the first number, 4. Line 3 asks: is 4 bigger than 4? No.
n moves to the next number, 9. Is 9 bigger than largest, 4? Yes.
Line 4 runs: largest becomes 9.
n moves to the last number, 2. Is 2 bigger than 9? No, so line 4 does not run.
No numbers remain. Line 5 reports largest. The screen shows 9.
You type python hello.py in the terminal and press Enter.
The terminal asks the operating system to run a command named python.
The operating system finds the Python interpreter and starts it with the file name hello.py.
The interpreter looks for hello.py in the current folder and opens it.
It reads line 1, the print instruction, and carries it out.
The interpreter sends the text to the terminal. The screen shows Hello, Ada.
No lines remain. The interpreter stops, and the terminal waits for your next command.
Line 1 stores the text apples in a jar labelled name. Line 2 stores 1.2 under price.
Line 3 stores the whole number 3 under count. Line 4 stores True under in_stock.
Every value has a type. The type decides what you can do with the value.
Line 5 reads price and count. Their values travel to the CPU.
The CPU multiplies 1.2 by 3 and gets 3.6.
The result goes into a new jar named cost.
Line 6 reads name and cost and prints them: apples cost 3.6.
A list is a row of numbered shelves. items holds apples, bread and milk at indexes 0, 1 and 2.
items[1] asks for shelf number 1. Python goes straight to it and returns bread.
items.append adds eggs at the end. It takes index 3, and len becomes 4.
A dictionary is a wall of labelled drawers. prices maps each name to its price.
prices['bread'] asks for the drawer labelled bread. Its position does not matter.
prices['eggs'] = 3.0 adds a drawer. Writing an existing key replaces its value instead.
Think first, second, third: use a list. Think the price of bread: use a dictionary.
Line 1 adds the three prices. total becomes 4.69.
Line 3 asks a yes-or-no question: is total greater than 4?
4.69 is greater than 4, so the condition gives the boolean True.
Two roads exist in the file. Python reads the sign once and takes only the True road.
The else block is skipped. The roads join, and the unindented print runs every time.
Change line 1 so total is 3.6. The question now gives False, and the other road runs.
One program, two behaviours, chosen by one condition.
prices holds three values. total starts at 0 before the loop.
Pass 1: price is set to the first item, 1.2.
The block adds price to total. total is 0 + 1.2 = 1.2.
Pass 2: price becomes 2.5. total is 1.2 + 2.5 = 3.7.
Pass 3: price becomes 0.99. total is 3.7 + 0.99 = 4.69.
No items remain, so the loop ends. The last print shows Final total: 4.69.
The interpreter reads the def block and remembers a function named basket_total. Nothing runs yet.
The main program calls basket_total(ada). The argument ada travels into the parameter prices.
The body sets total to 0, and the loop adds the three prices.
return total ends the body and hands 4.69 back. The local names prices and total vanish.
Back in the main program, the call stands for 4.69, and print shows Ada pays 4.69.
A second call, basket_total(sam), runs the same body with prices set to [3.0, 0.5].
It returns 3.5. One recipe card, two baskets, one line per call.
The program calls open with mode w. The operating system creates an empty file on the disk.
The loop writes the header line and 6 data lines. Each line ends with a newline character.
The with block ends and Python closes the file. The 7 lines are now safe on the disk.
A second program opens the file to read. csv.DictReader turns each line into a dictionary of strings.
Look at the quotes. The price is the string '150000'. The program converts it with int before it adds.
The loop adds the 6 prices one by one. The total counts up to 1,470,000.
Divide by the count, 6 houses. The mean is 245,000 pounds, the same as by hand.
Python prints a traceback with 3 parts: a header, one block per call, and the error line last.
Read the last line first. KeyError: 'Price' means a dictionary has no key named Price.
Go up one block. Line 8, inside the function mean_price, is the line that was running when it failed.
Is mean_price.py a file you wrote? Yes. So this is the line to fix.
The block above only called the function on line 12. It is not wrong, so leave it.
Compare the key Price with the header in the file: price. Fix the capital P and run again.

groupby('city') splits the rows by the value in the city column: 3 Leeds rows and 3 York rows.

Second, it finds the program. It checks each PATH folder in order: not here, not here, found in /bin.
Third, it runs the program /bin/cat and passes the argument cities.csv to it.

requests opens a connection and sends GET /v1/forecast across the internet to the Open-Meteo server.

The response comes back in three parts: a body, a Content-Type header and the status code 200.

response.json() turns the body into a Python dictionary. Follow the keys from the outside in: current.

Way 1. You write the 40-character key at the top of app.py. The program works at once.
You add, commit and push, as every day. The key travels to GitHub inside a public commit.

The Dockerfile has 5 lines. docker build -t weather . reads them from top to bottom.
FROM pulls the base image python:3.12-slim, about 150 MB, from Docker Hub. It is the first layer.
WORKDIR, COPY and RUN each add a layer: the folder /app, your files, and the requests library.
CMD is the last layer. It names the command to run later, not now. The image is complete and read-only.
docker run weather starts container 1, a fresh copy of the image, and runs python app.py inside it.
app.py prints three temperatures. The program ends and the container stops. The image did not change.
docker run weather again: a second, separate container starts from the same image and prints three new lines.
Your colleague runs the same image on a computer with no Python. Python 3.12 travels inside the image.
Row 3 is one example: one house that sold, written across the table in 5 cells.
The 4 cells that describe the house are features. Together they form X.
The price is the column we want to predict. It is the label, y.
A model reads the features, learns a rule, and compares its guess with the label.
Repeat for all 6 rows. The data set has 6 examples with 4 features: shape (6, 4).
Add the 6 prices and divide by 6. The mean price, 245,000 pounds, is a first guess for any house.
A model does arithmetic, so it reads only numbers. The size 90 goes in as it is.
York is a category from a fixed list. It becomes one 0/1 code per option: Leeds 0, York 1.
The binary column garden maps no to 0 and yes to 1.
The door photo is not in the table. Cut it into a grid of 4 by 4 pixels.
Each pixel holds a brightness from 0 (black) to 255 (white). The dark handle is the two 60s.
The 16 numbers go to the model as one list. Their mean, 173.75, says the door is bright.
Look first. The raw table has 8 rows. The mean, 535,000, is more than twice the median, 235,000.
Fix formats. strip and title turn YORK and leeds into York and Leeds. 4 spellings become 2.
Drop duplicates. Row 7 is an exact copy of row 2 and goes away. 7 rows remain.
Fill the missing value. Houses of 85 to 100 square metres have 3 bedrooms, so row 3 gets 3.
Check outliers. Row 8 costs 30,588 pounds per square metre, 10 times the other houses.
The agent confirms the real price was 260,000. Fix it. The mean falls to 247,143, close to the median.
Look again. 7 rows, 2 cities, no missing cells, mean and median close. The table is clean.
The agent's first file has 8 columns. Three of them point to real people.
Check the source. Names come from her private sales book. Prices were checked against the public Land Registry.
Check the licence. Land Registry prices are open under the OGL. The names and phones have no licence.
Find personal data. Drop seller and phone. Replace the address with the city, which identifies nobody.
Count for bias. 3 rows in Leeds, 3 in York, 0 anywhere else. All sizes sit between 50 and 120.
Price per square metre is about 3,000 in both cities. A London flat costs 8,571. The table never saw London.
Write the datasheet: source, licence, columns removed, rows per group, known gaps. Only then may the model train.
The test share on the report card is the fraction 1/5. Three shapes can write this one amount.
Divide the top by the bottom: 1 divided by 5 gives the decimal 0.2.
Multiply the decimal by 100 and add the sign: 20 percent. Same amount, third shape.
The parameters line is huge. Programs write 7e9: start with 7 and move the point 9 places right.
The learning rate is tiny. In 3e-4 the point moves 4 places left: 0.0003.
Each shape is the best way to write one kind of amount. Read the shape before the digits.
A function is a machine: one number in, one number out. This is the taxi meter f.
Put the input x = 5 into the machine, a ride of 5 kilometres.
Inside, the rule runs: double 5 to get 10, then add 3 to get 13.
So f(5) = 13 euros. Put 5 in again and 13 comes out again.
The output of f becomes the input of a second machine, the tip t.
The tip machine multiplies by 1.1: t(13) = 14.3 euros. One machine feeding another is composition.
Swap the order and you get a different machine: f(t(5)) = 14, not 14.3.
Five houses. Size goes across, price goes up. Each house is one point.
Pick two points far apart, A and E. Go across first: the run is 130 minus 50, which is 80.
Then go up: the rise is 330 minus 150, which is 180.
Slope is rise over run: 180 divided by 80 is 2.25. Each extra square metre adds 2.25 thousand euros.
Put house A into y = mx + b: 150 = 2.25 times 50 plus b, so b = 37.5.
Draw the line y = 2.25x + 37.5. It passes through A and E and runs close to the others.
Your line by eye, y = 2.3x + 35, is almost the same. Give it 100: it predicts 265.
The loss halves every 1,000 steps: 8, 4, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125.
On a normal scale the curve flattens. The last three points look the same, but the halving continues.
Ask each loss a new question: 2 to the power of what gives it? For 8, that is 3.
Each halving subtracts 1 from the answer: 3, 2, 1, 0, -1, -2, -3. Both dots move together.
On the log scale the seven points lie on a straight line. Its slope is minus 1 per 1,000 steps.
A straight line on a log scale means steady progress. That is why loss curves are drawn with logs.
Here is House A. Fix three features in this order: rooms, floors, kilometres to school.
Count the rooms: 3. Write 3 in the first slot.
Count the floors: 2. Write 2 in the second slot.
Measure the distance to the school: 1 kilometre. Write 1 in the third slot. The list has dimension 3.
Keep only [3, 2] to draw it. Start at the origin, go 3 right, then 2 up.
That spot is the point [3, 2]. An arrow from the origin to it is the same list.
Here are a = [3, 4] and b = [1, 2], two arrows from the origin.
To add them, slide b so that its tail sits on the tip of a.
The sum runs from the origin to the new tip: (3 + 1, 4 + 2) = (4, 6).
Multiply a by 2. Every component doubles. The arrow keeps its direction and is twice as long.
Back to a. Walk 3 east, then 4 north. With a, that makes a right-angled triangle.
Square and add the two sides: 9 plus 16 is 25. The square root, 5, is the norm of a.
The distance from b to a is the norm of a - b: square root of 8, about 2.83.
Take a = [3, 4] and b = [1, 2]. Multiply the components that sit in the same position.
First position: 3 times 1 is 3.
Second position: 4 times 2 is 8.
Add the products: 3 plus 8 is 11. The dot product of a and b is one scalar, 11.
Draw both arrows. They point almost the same way, so the dot product is large and positive.
Divide 11 by both norms, 5 and 2.236. The cosine similarity is 0.98: almost the same direction.
Turn b until it stands at a right angle to a. The dot product falls to 0: orthogonal.
Here is the rotation matrix R with two rows, and the vector v = [3, 4] as an arrow.
Row 1 dot v: 0 times 3 plus minus 1 times 4 is minus 4.
Row 2 dot v: 1 times 3 plus 0 times 4 is 3.
Stack the two results: Rv = [-4, 3]. The arrow turns a quarter turn to the left.
Check the length: 16 plus 9 is 25, square root 5. R turned v but kept its length.
Swap in the stretch matrix S. The same rule sends [3, 4] to [6, 4], a longer arrow.
Multiply A by B. Inner numbers 2 and 2 match, so the product exists and is 2 by 2.
Row 1 of A with column 1 of B: 1 times 1 plus 2 times 2 is 5.
Row 1 of A with column 2 of B: 1 times 0 plus 2 times 1 is 2.
Row 2 of A with column 1 of B: 3 times 1 plus 4 times 2 is 11.
Row 2 of A with column 2 of B: 3 times 0 plus 4 times 1 is 4.
Read AB: first row 5 and 2, second row 11 and 4. Four entries cost eight multiplications.
Swap the order. The matrices change places, and BA has first row 1, 2 and second row 5, 8.
The car's position is p(t) = t squared. We want its speed at exactly t = 1.
A second point at t = 3 makes a gap h of 2. The line through both is a secant.
The slope of the secant is the rise over the run: 8 metres over 2 seconds, which is 4.
Shrink the gap. Slide the second point to t = 2. The average falls to 3.
Shrink again to t = 1.5, then to t = 1.1. The averages go 2.5, then 2.1.
With h = 0.01 the average is 2.01. The averages head for 2 and never pass it.
At the limit the secant becomes the tangent at (1, 1). Its slope, 2, is the derivative.
A function inside a function: x goes into the inner part, and its output u goes into the outer part.
Put in x = 0. The inner part gives u = -3. The outer part squares it: f = 9.
The inner rate: u grows by 1 when x grows by 1. The inner slope is 1.
The outer rate: u squared changes by 2u per unit of u. At u = -3 that is -6.
Like the currency chain, multiply the two rates: -6 times 1 is -6.
The same chain at any x gives 2(x - 3). At x = 0 that is exactly -6.
The valley is (x - 3) squared. Start at x = 0: f is 9 and the slope is -6.
With learning rate 0.1 the step is 0.1 times -6, which is -0.6. Subtract it: x becomes 0.6.
Feel the slope again: -4.8. The next steps are -0.48 and -0.384. The steps shrink as the slope shrinks.
Start again at x = 0 with learning rate 0.5. The step is 0.5 times -6, which is -3.
One stride lands exactly at x = 3. The slope is 0 and f is 0: finished in one step.
Start again with learning rate 1.2. The step is -7.2, so x jumps over the valley to 7.2.
The slope is now 8.4 and the step 10.08. x lands at -2.88, f grows to 34.57. The walk diverges.
The bowl has its bottom at (0, 0). Start at (3, 1), where f is 11.
Hold y fixed and feel the slope along x. The partial derivative is 2x, which is 6 here.
Hold x fixed and feel the slope along y. The partial derivative is 4y, which is 4.
Put the two numbers together: the gradient [6, 4]. It points straight uphill, away from the bottom.
Multiply the gradient by the learning rate 0.1. The arrow shrinks to [0.6, 0.4].
Subtract it: the arrow flips to point downhill. The point moves to (2.4, 0.6) and f falls to 6.48.
Repeat. Each step multiplies x by 0.8 and y by 0.6, so the point heads for the bottom.
Roll a red and a blue die. Each cell is one pair of faces: 6 times 6 is 36 outcomes.
Both show 6 in one cell. The dice are independent: 1/6 times 1/6 is 1/36, about 0.028.
At least one 6: the last row and the last column, corner counted once. That is 11 cells, 11/36.
The complement is easier. Mark the cells with no 6 at all: 5 times 5 is 25 cells.
Subtract from the whole pie: 1 minus 25/36 is 11/36, about 0.306. Both ways agree.
Check the rules: 0.306 lies between 0 and 1, and 25/36 plus 11/36 is 1.
A company sorts 1,000 emails into spam or not, and checks each one for the word free.
Before any clue, 200 of the 1,000 emails are spam. The base rate is 0.2.
A new email contains free. Zoom in on that column: only 190 emails remain.
Inside the column, 150 of the 190 emails are spam.
Divide 150 by 190: P(spam given free) is 0.789. The clue raised it from 0.2.
Bayes' rule gives the same answer: 0.75 times 0.2, divided by 0.19, is 0.789.
Now make spam rare: 1 percent of 10,000 emails. The same clue gives only 0.13.
Six days of email: 3, 5, 6, 6, 8 and 14. Each count is a dot on a number line.
Add them: 42. Divide by 6: the mean is 7, the balance point of the line.
Measure each distance from the mean: -4, -2, -1, -1, 1 and 7. They add up to 0.
Square each distance: 16, 4, 1, 1, 1 and 49. The sum is 72, and 72 over 6 is 12.
The square root of 12 is 3.46: the standard deviation, the typical distance from the mean.
A second list, 6, 7, 7, 7, 7, 8, also adds up to 42, so its mean is also 7.
Its distances are -1, 0, 0, 0, 0 and 1. The squares add up to 2: variance 0.33.
Its standard deviation is 0.58. Same mean, much less spread: the second inbox is predictable.
The model gives one raw score per class: cat 2, dog 1 and bird 0.
Raise e to each score. The scores become 7.389, 2.718 and 1.000, all positive.
Add the three results: 7.389 plus 2.718 plus 1.000 is 11.107.
Divide each result by the sum. Cat gets 7.389 over 11.107, which is 0.665.
Dog gets 2.718 over 11.107, which is 0.245. Bird gets 1 over 11.107, which is 0.090.
The three add up to 1: a categorical distribution. Cat still leads, and the gaps grew.
Double the scores to 4, 2, 0. Softmax gets sharper: cat 0.867, dog 0.117, bird 0.016.
Surprise is minus log base 2 of a probability. The curve climbs steeply as the probability falls.
The model predicted cat 0.665, dog 0.245 and bird 0.090. The photo shows a cat.
A sure right answer costs 0 bits. Slide to 0.665, the cat probability: the loss is 0.589 bits.
Now suppose the photo shows a bird. The model gave bird only 0.090.
The same prediction now costs 3.474 bits. Confidence in a wrong answer is punished hard.
A batch of 3 photos gives its true class 0.665, 0.5 and 0.1: surprises 0.589, 1 and 3.322.
The training loss is the mean: 4.911 over 3 is 1.637 bits. Training pushes every dot down the curve.
A staff member asks where to submit an expense receipt. Start with a specific task. A general request to add AI does not define success.
The workflow finds the current approved procedure. The model needs relevant evidence. A confident answer from memory can still be outdated or wrong.
The model drafts an answer using the supplied procedure. Drafting creates wording. It does not approve a payment or change the source policy.
A staff member checks the draft against the source. The reviewer looks for invented promises, omitted conditions, and the wrong document version.
The staff member shares the checked response. The final action uses the normal service process. The person remains responsible for the message.
The email Free meeting tomorrow arrives. It has three words.
The rule filter looks for the word free. It finds it, so it says spam. That is wrong.
The learned filter has a share for each word, counted from 1,000 marked emails. Nobody typed them.
It adds the three shares: 0.87 plus 0.03 plus 0.10 is 1.00.
Divide by the 3 known words. The average is 0.33, which is below the 0.5 line.
So the learned filter says normal. That is right: meeting and tomorrow pulled the score down.
This curve is the loss for every value of w. Lower is better. The model cannot see it.
Start with the guess w equals 2. The loss there is 7,650: every prediction is too low.
The slope under the ball is minus 14,800. A negative slope means the loss falls when w grows.
Update: w moves by minus 0.00005 times the slope, which is plus 0.74. The ball rolls to 2.74.
The loss is 668. The slope is smaller, so the step is smaller: w becomes 2.94, loss 140.
One more step: w reaches 3.00 and the loss is 100. The slope is nearly zero, so the steps stop.
Evaluate on a house not in the table: 80 square metres. The model says 240; it sold for 250.
You type: which house has a garden and costs under 250 thousand? The chat app sends it to the agent.
The agent plans. It needs house data, so it asks retrieval, which returns the three listings with gardens.
The agent sends the listings and the question to the model server. Inference runs with fixed parameters.
The model does not run tools. It returns a tool request: filter_houses, garden yes, max price 250.
The agent runs the tool, a 5-line Python function over the table. It returns house 2 only.
The agent sends the result back. The model writes the final sentence: house 2 in Leeds, 210 thousand.
The chat app shows the answer. Monitoring writes one log line: 812 input tokens, 64 output tokens, 1.4 seconds.
Each house is one point: size across, price up. Here are the 5 houses.
Average the sizes and the prices. The mean point sits at size 80 and price 208.
The best line passes through the mean point, with slope w = 2.5 and intercept b = 8.
Each house sits a little off the line. The gaps are the residuals, and they add up to 0.
Square each residual, add, divide by 5: the MSE is 56. No other line gets a smaller MSE.
Now predict a 90 square metre house: slide along the line to size 90 and read 233.
The 5 houses again. The question: how well does the line price a house it has never seen?
Hide house 3 before fitting. The other 4 houses are the training set.
Fit the line to the 4 training houses only: price = 2.5 times size + 5.
Each training residual is 5 or minus 5. Square, add and divide by 4: training MSE 25.
Now bring back house 3. The line predicts 205 for 80 square metres, but it sold for 220.
The test residual is 15. Squared, the test MSE is 225, nine times the training MSE.
The line gives each size a score z. The sigmoid squashes z into a probability p between 0 and 1.
The 5 houses sit on the curve at their sizes. The dashed line is the threshold, 0.5.
House 1, 40 square metres: z = 3.5, p = 0.971. Above the threshold, so predict yes. Correct.
Slide to house 2 at 60 square metres: z = 1.5 and p = 0.818. Predict yes. Correct.
House 3, 80 square metres: p = 0.378, below the line. Predict no. But it really sold fast: a miss.
Houses 4 and 5 give p = 0.076 and 0.011. Predict no, and both really were no. Correct.
Four of five right: accuracy 0.8. The one error is a miss, not a false alarm.
A tree asks one question: is the size at most a cut? Here are the 5 houses it must split.
Try the cut at 50. The left side predicts its mean, 110. The right side predicts 232.5.
Score the cut: add the squared residuals of both sides. 0 plus 13275 is 13275.
Move the cut to 70. The means become 130 and 260, and the score falls to 5000.
Move it to 90. The means are 160 and 280, and the score rises to 8000. Worse.
Move it to 110. The score rises again, to 12275. Worse still.
The cut at 70 has the smallest score, so the root question is: size at most 70?
The tree repeats the search on the right and cuts at 110. Three leaves predict 130, 235 and 310.
The same 5 houses. Three models try to learn the pattern: a mean, a line and a degree-4 curve.
The mean model predicts 208 for every house. Training MSE 5056: too simple to see the pattern.
The straight line follows the trend. Its training MSE is 56.
The degree-4 curve passes through all 5 points exactly. Training MSE 0. It looks perfect.
Then 2 new houses sell: 50 square metres for 140, and 110 square metres for 290.

The image is 640 by 480 pixels. The principal point (320, 240) sits at its centre.
A block corner sits 0.1 m right, 0.05 m down, and 0.5 m in front of the camera.
Divide X and Y by Z: 0.1 / 0.5 = 0.2 and 0.05 / 0.5 = 0.1.
Multiply by the focal length of 500 pixels: 100 and 50 pixels from the centre.
Add the principal point: u = 320 + 100 = 420 and v = 240 + 50 = 290.
Move the block to Z = 1.0 m. Every offset halves and the pixel becomes (370, 265).
Twice as far from the camera means half as far from the image centre.
Two lenses sit 6 cm apart. This distance is the baseline. Each has a focal length of 500 pixels.
A cup stands 0.5 m in front. Each camera sees it along its own ray.
The left camera sees the cup at column 400. The right camera sees it at column 340.
The difference is the disparity: 400 - 340 = 60 pixels.
Depth is f times b over d: 500 x 0.06 / 60 = 0.5 m.
Move the cup to 2.0 m. The rays turn almost parallel and the disparity drops to 15 pixels.
The matcher is off by one pixel and reports 14. The depth becomes 2.14 m, an error of 14 cm.
At 0.5 m the same one-pixel error gives 8 mm. Stereo error grows with the square of distance.
The robot starts at 0 m and moves at 1 m/s. We estimate its position once per second.
Predict: the motion model moves the estimate to 1.0 m. Wheel slip adds variance Q = 0.04.
Measure: the camera reports 1.3 m. Its variance R = 0.09 is larger, so it earns less trust.
The Kalman gain is P over P plus R: 0.04 / 0.13 = 0.31.
Update: the estimate moves 31 percent of the way to the measurement, to 1.09 m.
The variance shrinks: (1 - 0.31) x 0.04 = 0.028. Two sources beat one.
Predict again: the estimate becomes 2.09 m and the variance grows to 0.028 + 0.04 = 0.068.
The joint starts at 0 degrees. The setpoint is 90. The error is 90 - 0 = 90.
Step 1: the P term is 45, the I term 0.9, the D term 0. Command 45.9 V.
The joint moves to 30 degrees. The error falls to 60.
Step 2: P = 30, I = 1.5. The error fell fast, so D = 0.2 x (-300) = -60.
The command is 30 + 1.5 - 60 = -28.5 V. The derivative term brakes the joint.
The joint moves to 50 degrees. Error 40, P 20, I 1.9, D -40. Command -18.1 V.
Without the D term, the step-2 command is 31.5 V and the joint passes 90 and comes back.

You type a question in the browser. It goes to the API server.
The server turns the question into numbers and asks the vector database for similar text.
The database returns the five closest chunks.
The server builds a prompt from the question and the chunks and sends it to the model.
The model writes an answer. The server streams it back to you.
This is the loss curve. Low is good. The model cannot see the whole curve, only where it stands.
Start anywhere, say at x = 0, where the loss is 9.
Measure the slope under the ball. It is minus 6: the curve falls to the right.
Step the other way: new x = x minus 0.1 times the slope. The ball rolls downhill.
Repeat. Each step is smaller because the slope shrinks near the bottom.
At the minimum the slope is zero, so the steps stop. That is what training does, millions of times.
A vector is an arrow from the origin. Its two numbers say how far to go right and up.
Here is a second vector, b.
To add vectors, slide b so it starts at the tip of a.
The sum goes from the origin to the tip of the moved arrow: (3 + 1, 1 + 2) = (4, 3).
Multiplying by a number scales the arrow. 2a points the same way and is twice as long.
